title: Why Astronauts Float in Space (Gravity Is Still 90% Strong!)
description: Gravity on the International Space Station is about 90% as strong as on Earth's surface, so why do astronauts float? The answer is free fall, and it changes how you think about orbit. Here is the real physics in under 90 seconds.

scenes.narration: Astronauts on the space station float around like gravity doesn't exist. But here's the crazy part: gravity up there is still about 90 percent as strong as on Earth.
scenes.search_keyword: astronaut floating | space station interior | earth from space

scenes.narration: The station orbits roughly 400 kilometers up. That's tiny compared to Earth's radius of about 6,400 kilometers, so Earth's pull barely weakens.
scenes.search_keyword: earth orbit view | satellite over earth | globe model

scenes.narration: So why the floating? Because the station and everyone inside it are in constant free fall.
scenes.search_keyword: falling skydiver | space station orbit | astronaut spacewalk

scenes.narration: Imagine standing in an elevator while the cable snaps. You and the elevator fall together, so you'd feel weightless.
scenes.search_keyword: elevator doors | elevator interior | skyscraper looking up

scenes.narration: The station is doing the same thing, but it's also moving sideways at about 28,000 kilometers per hour.
scenes.search_keyword: rocket launch | speedometer closeup | earth curvature

scenes.narration: That sideways speed is the key. As the station falls toward Earth, the planet's surface curves away beneath it, so it keeps missing the ground.
scenes.search_keyword: earth horizon | cannon firing | planet curvature

scenes.narration: That endless fall is what we call an orbit. The station circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so the crew sees around 16 sunrises a day.
scenes.search_keyword: sunrise from space | astronaut window | night earth lights

scenes.narration: So astronauts aren't floating because gravity is gone. They're floating because they're falling along with everything around them. Did you know this before, or did it surprise you? Tell me in the comments!
